title: The Space Between Work and AI
excerpt: Building Newton has made me think about a persistent, personal layer between AI models and the work they help us do.
html:
I’ve spent a lot of time lately thinking about what it actually means to work with AI, mostly because building Newton has forced me to think about it in ways I hadn’t before.

Tools like ChatGPT and cloud coding agents are already very good at giving us a place to start. You open a session, explain what you’re trying to do, work through it, generate some code or an artifact, make changes, and eventually get somewhere useful.

I use that workflow constantly. But the more I use it, the more I notice a gap between what the AI needs in order to do the work and what I need in order to actually work with it.

An AI is pretty comfortable with context, instructions, files and tools. As a person, I tend to want something more concrete. I want to know what’s happening, where things live, what needs my attention and what I’m supposed to do next.

There are really two different questions in there: What do I need this thing to do, and how do I want to experience using it?

That distinction has gradually become a big part of what Newton is.

From a session to a workspace

The easiest way I’ve found to think about Newton is as a team and a workspace.

The team is the AI. Different parts of it can have different roles, context, responsibilities and tools. Whether those are technically separate agents, prompts, models or processes isn’t particularly important to me as the person using it. I just need to understand who is doing what and be able to work with them that way.

The workspace is the other half. It’s the part built around me.

Sometimes I want a board. Sometimes I need a dashboard, an approval queue, a calendar or a document. Sometimes the right interface is something specific enough to the work that it doesn’t really fit into an existing category.

The AI probably doesn’t need any of that structure. I do.

That sounds like a small distinction, but it changes how I think about building software around AI. Instead of starting with an interface and figuring out how to put AI into it, I can start with what I need to accomplish and then decide what interacting with that should actually feel like.

The longevity problem

There’s another part of the gap that I didn’t really recognize until I started building more of these things: longevity.

At least for me, artifacts are mostly disposable.

I’ll be working through something with an AI, realize I need a document, an interface, a visualization, whatever, and make one. I might use it for a while or iterate on it a few times, but it usually belongs to that particular session and that particular problem.

That works really well when the need is temporary. A lot of my needs aren’t.

If I make a project dashboard that turns out to be genuinely useful, I don’t want to make another one next week. I want that dashboard to become part of how I work. I want to come back to it, change it over time, and have the context around it continue to accumulate.

I think that’s where I started seeing the difference between an artifact and what I’m trying to do with Newton. It’s not that artifacts need to become permanent, or that every useful AI interaction needs to turn into software. Sometimes you just discover something useful enough that it stops being an output and starts becoming part of your environment.

The conversation can be temporary. The thing I figured out I need might not be.

Building the layer in between

For a while, I think I treated the interface and the AI as more or less the same product. You open ChatGPT and talk to the AI. You open a coding agent and build with the AI. The software is basically the window through which you access the intelligence.

But as the underlying models get more capable, I’m finding myself less interested in the window.

If I can describe what I need the AI to do, I should also be able to decide how I want to interact with the result. I don’t necessarily need someone else’s idea of a project manager, inbox, dashboard or workflow just because that happens to be the software wrapped around the model.

That layer can become much more personal.

And I think this is what I’ve actually been discovering while building Newton. It didn’t start with some grand plan for an AI platform. I kept building small things, using them, finding friction and changing them. A useful interaction became a role. A role needed somewhere to live. That place needed an interface. Some of those interfaces turned out to be useful enough that I wanted to keep them.

Eventually those decisions started looking less like a collection of AI tools and more like an environment.

That’s the part of Newton I’m most interested in now. Not replacing ChatGPT, coding agents or artifacts, because I still use all of them. It’s figuring out what happens when something discovered through those tools needs to last longer than the session that created it.

The models underneath all of this are going to keep changing. The way we interact with them probably will too. What I’m increasingly interested in is the layer between those models and me: something persistent enough to accumulate context, flexible enough to change with the work, and specific enough to reflect how I actually want to work.

Newton is what I’ve been building in that space.

title: Creative work, fewer tools
excerpt: What connects an AI workspace, a rhyme studio, a photo library, and a gaming case? An interest in making the tools around creative work feel more useful—and less demanding.
html:
My projects cover a lot of ground: websites, identities, apparel, live broadcasts, interactive experiences, physical products, and software. Working on this portfolio has given me a reason to look at them together. A recurring interest has become clearer: I like making things, and I like improving the tools that help people make things.

That second part is becoming a larger part of my work.

Creative projects often come with a surprising amount of coordination. A conversation lives in one app, the files in another, and the useful reference somewhere in a browser tab. Before you can do the next piece of work, you have to find the right material and remember how it all fits together. Each tool might do its own job well, but moving between them becomes a job of its own.

That is the kind of software bloat I’m interested in reducing. Overlapping features are part of it. So are repeated setup, duplicated information, and interfaces that require more attention than the task deserves. I want to build tools around a coherent activity and keep the things that belong together close enough to be useful.

Newton is one version of that idea. I’m building a desktop workspace for persistent AI teammates, bringing projects, conversations, roles, and recurring work into one place. It connects tools such as Codex CLI and Claude Code within a shared workspace. The design question is how to make that work easier to return to: what was happening, who was handling it, and what needs attention next? Keeping that context available is a big part of what I want Newton to do well.

Current approaches the same problem on a much shorter timescale. It’s a live rhyme studio that connects spoken or typed words with rhyme suggestions, related sounds, and phrase ideas. When you’re working on a line, a useful suggestion has a very small window to be helpful. I’m exploring how to keep those suggestions nearby while leaving room for the person using it to follow their own train of thought. The rhyme log, audio, and transcript tools also give the session somewhere to go afterward.

Vispix comes from another familiar part of creative work: choosing images. A photo library becomes more useful when you can search it, review options with a team, understand usage rights, and build a shortlist in the same place. Vispix brings those activities together. Its connection to AI tools extends access to the existing library, so the photos and their information can be useful within other workflows too.

These projects share a design challenge. Every additional feature has to earn the space it takes up. Putting five disconnected tools inside one window would still leave a lot of coordination to the user. The useful work is deciding what should share context, what should happen automatically, and what needs a clear human decision. A focused tool needs boundaries, and maintaining those boundaries is part of building it.

I can trace that interest through my earlier work as well. Producing live broadcasts for USA Archery involves graphics, scoring data, audio, video, and on-site production. I’ve built custom software to support that process and connect real-time scoring to the broadcast. In that setting, an interface has to make sense while an event is happening. The visual design and the underlying system have to work together under the same constraints.

PlayCase brings the question into the physical world. It adds real controls to an iPhone for playing classic games, with swappable faceplates for different button layouts. The work spans industrial design, prototyping, production, and the way the product is presented. It’s another example of how much the experience can change when you reconsider the interface between a person and something they already use.

There’s also room for exploration. With Arcadia, I’m investigating how an AI workspace and a simulated world might relate to each other—how software activity could become something you can see and navigate as a place. That gives me room to think about character, presence, and play alongside practical questions about coordination.

Newton and Current are still in active development, and Arcadia is an ongoing experiment. I’m working through where consolidation helps and where a tool should stay small. Building the software creates its own maintenance work, so reducing friction has to remain something I evaluate, rather than something I assume.

This is where creative work and technology meet for me. Understanding the activity helps me shape the interface; building the system lets me test whether that design actually helps. Across these projects, I want to make it easier to stay with an idea, find what it needs, and carry it through to something finished.
